entries.meaning: Shaped like the letter V, wide at the top and narrow at the bottom. ---
examples: The trail follows a V-shaped valley.
She wore a sweater with a V-shaped neckline.
Geese fly in a V-shaped formation.
entries.contrast: Written with a capital V and a hyphen: a V-shaped valley. Economists use it for a downturn that rebounds just as fast as it fell.

entries.meaning: Vacant has 3 distinct senses.
examples: There's a vacant lot behind the store.
Two apartments in the building are vacant.
The seat has been vacant since March.
They're advertising a vacant teaching position.
He gave me a vacant stare.
Her expression went vacant for a second.

senses.head: Empty and available; not occupied
examples: There's a vacant lot behind the store.
Two apartments in the building are vacant.

senses.head: Of a job or a position: not filled
examples: The seat has been vacant since March.
They're advertising a vacant teaching position.

senses.head: Showing no thought or interest
examples: He gave me a vacant stare.
Her expression went vacant for a second.

entries.contrast: Vacant means empty and available: a vacant room can be taken. Empty only says there is nothing in it.

entries.meaning: Having been given a vaccine to protect against a disease. ---
examples: All the kids are fully vaccinated.
Are you vaccinated against hepatitis?
Vaccinated travelers skip the extra paperwork.

entries.meaning: Vacuous has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The speech was polished but vacuous.
He asked a string of vacuous questions.
She wore a vacuous smile the whole time.
His face went vacuous when we asked for details.

senses.head: Empty of ideas or meaning; silly
examples: The speech was polished but vacuous.
He asked a string of vacuous questions.

senses.head: Showing no thought or feeling, of a look or a smile
examples: She wore a vacuous smile the whole time.
His face went vacuous when we asked for details.

entries.meaning: Relating to the vagina. ---
examples: She had a vaginal delivery.
The pharmacy stocks several vaginal medications.
Vaginal infections are usually easy to treat.

entries.meaning: Vague has 3 distinct senses.
examples: He gave a vague answer about the schedule.
Their plans are still pretty vague.
The instructions got vaguer the further I read.
I have a vague memory of the house.
She had a vague sense that something was wrong.
He was vague about where the money went.
She's a little vague before her coffee.

senses.head: Not clear or exact; short on detail
examples: He gave a vague answer about the schedule.
Their plans are still pretty vague.
The instructions got vaguer the further I read.

senses.head: Slight; not strong or definite, of a feeling or a memory
examples: I have a vague memory of the house.
She had a vague sense that something was wrong.

senses.head: Of a person: not giving details, or not thinking clearly
examples: He was vague about where the money went.
She's a little vague before her coffee.

entries.takes: about + noun or -ing when it describes a person (vague about the details)

entries.meaning: Vain has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He's vain about his hair.
She's the vainest person I know.
It was a vain attempt to save the building.
They made one last vain effort to reach him by phone.

senses.head: Too proud of your looks or your abilities
examples: He's vain about his hair.
She's the vainest person I know.

senses.head: Unsuccessful; producing no result
examples: It was a vain attempt to save the building.
They made one last vain effort to reach him by phone.

entries.position: both — the 'useless' sense only before a noun: a vain attempt
entries.contrast: Three homophones: vain (тщеславный), vein (вена) and vane (флюгер). In vain means 'without success': They searched in vain.

entries.meaning: Very brave and determined, especially against long odds. ---
examples: They made a valiant effort to keep the store open.
He was valiant in the face of a terrible diagnosis.
The firefighters got a medal for their valiant work.
entries.contrast: Formal or literary; everyday English says brave. It is very common in a valiant effort, which is usually said of a try that failed.

entries.meaning: Valid has 2 distinct senses.
examples: You need a valid driver's license.
The coupon is valid through Sunday.
That's a valid point.
She had a valid reason for missing the exam.

senses.head: Officially or legally acceptable
examples: You need a valid driver's license.
The coupon is valid through Sunday.

senses.head: Based on good reasoning; fair
examples: That's a valid point.
She had a valid reason for missing the exam.

entries.takes: for + a period or a purpose (valid for six months)
entries.contrast: The opposite is stressed in-VAL-id when it means 'not valid'; the noun invalid, a person too sick to care for themselves, is stressed IN-vuh-lid.

entries.meaning: Validated has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Only validated results go into the report.
The lab uses a validated testing method.
She felt validated when the doctor finally believed her.
It feels good to be validated by people you respect.

senses.head: Officially checked and confirmed
examples: Only validated results go into the report.
The lab uses a validated testing method.

senses.head: Feeling that your feelings or your experience have been recognized as real
examples: She felt validated when the doctor finally believed her.
It feels good to be validated by people you respect.

entries.meaning: Valuable has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The ring is quite valuable.
Lock your valuable equipment in the van.
That was valuable advice.
She's the most valuable person on the team.

senses.head: Worth a lot of money
examples: The ring is quite valuable.
Lock your valuable equipment in the van.

senses.head: Very useful or important
examples: That was valuable advice.
She's the most valuable person on the team.

entries.takes: to + a person (valuable to us); for + noun or -ing
entries.contrast: Invaluable is not the opposite of valuable — it means so useful that no price fits: Her advice was invaluable. The plural noun valuables means jewelry, money and the like.

entries.meaning: Treated as important and appreciated. ---
examples: Thank you for being a valued customer.
Employees need to feel valued.
He was a valued member of the department.
entries.position: both — before a noun in a valued customer, after a verb in feel valued
entries.contrast: Valued means appreciated by people; valuable means worth a lot of money. Watch for the verb as well: a painting valued at $2 million means someone set that price.

entries.meaning: Ordinary, with no special features. ---
examples: It's a pretty vanilla setup — nothing custom.
They offered a plain vanilla version of the loan.
The movie was vanilla but pleasant enough.
entries.contrast: In vanilla ice cream and vanilla extract this is the noun, the flavor. As an adjective it is informal and means 'plain, with no special features', usually about products, software or plans.

entries.meaning: Dull and empty of interest or ideas. ---
examples: The interview was a string of vapid questions.
I couldn't sit through another vapid reality show.
Her lyrics are catchy but vapid.
entries.contrast: Formal and dismissive, close to vacuous, but used more about talk, writing and entertainment than about faces.

entries.meaning: Variable has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The weather here is highly variable.
Service has been variable at best.
The drill has a variable speed setting.
They offer a variable interest rate.

senses.head: Likely to change; not staying the same
examples: The weather here is highly variable.
Service has been variable at best.

senses.head: Able to be set at different levels
examples: The drill has a variable speed setting.
They offer a variable interest rate.

entries.contrast: Also a noun in math and science (solve for the variable). Variable means it changes; various means several different ones.

entries.meaning: Of a vein: swollen and twisted, usually in the legs. ---
examples: She's having her varicose veins treated.
Varicose veins run in my family.
Standing all day can make varicose veins worse.
entries.position: attributive only — almost always in varicose veins

entries.meaning: Made up of many different kinds; not all the same. ---
examples: The menu is more varied than it looks.
He's had a long and varied career.
Reviews have been varied.
entries.contrast: Varied describes a range that holds many kinds (a varied menu); various means 'several different' and goes straight before a plural noun (various reasons).

entries.meaning: Several different. ---
examples: We looked at various options before deciding.
She's lived in various cities over the years.
The delay was caused by various problems at the port.
entries.position: attributive only — straight before a plural noun: various reasons
entries.contrast: Various replaces the article: for various reasons, never for a various reason. It does not follow be in everyday English — say The reasons vary. And it is not varied, which is about a rich range.

entries.meaning: Different from one case to the next; changing in amount or degree. ---
examples: The programs work, with varying degrees of success.
Students arrive with varying levels of preparation.
The pills come in varying strengths.
entries.contrast: Nearly fixed in varying degrees, varying amounts and varying levels. For something that keeps changing, use variable.

entries.meaning: Relating to the tubes that carry blood in the body or sap in a plant. ---
examples: He sees a vascular surgeon twice a year.
Smoking raises the risk of vascular disease.
Ferns are vascular plants.

entries.meaning: Extremely large in area, amount or range. ---
examples: The vast majority of readers never comment.
They crossed a vast stretch of desert.
Up close, the canyon felt even vaster than in the pictures.
entries.comparison: -er/-est or more/most — vaster, vastest, more vast
entries.contrast: Very common in the vast majority (подавляющее большинство). The comparative forms are rare — most writers say far vaster or switch to huge.

entries.meaning: Built with a high, curved or arched ceiling. ---
examples: The living room has a vaulted ceiling.
We ate under the vaulted arches of the old market.
The chapel's vaulted roof is the oldest part of the building.

entries.meaning: Vegan has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The restaurant has a separate vegan menu.
Is the chocolate cake vegan?
She's been vegan for five years.
Half the people at the dinner were vegan.

senses.head: Containing no meat, fish, dairy, eggs or other animal products
examples: The restaurant has a separate vegan menu.
Is the chocolate cake vegan?

senses.head: Eating and using no animal products at all
examples: She's been vegan for five years.
Half the people at the dinner were vegan.

entries.contrast: Vegan excludes all animal products; vegetarian excludes only meat and fish. It is also a noun (a vegan), and Americans say both she's vegan and she's a vegan. The first syllable is VEE, not VAY.

entries.meaning: Vegetative has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He was in a vegetative state for two years.
Doctors distinguish a vegetative state from a coma.
The plant is still in its vegetative stage.
Vegetative growth slows once the buds open.

senses.head: Of a patient: alive but showing no awareness — in a vegetative state
examples: He was in a vegetative state for two years.
Doctors distinguish a vegetative state from a coma.

senses.head: Of a plant: growing leaves and stems rather than flowers or seeds
examples: The plant is still in its vegetative stage.
Vegetative growth slows once the buds open.

entries.meaning: Showing strong, forceful feeling, especially in opposition. ---
examples: She was vehement in her denial.
The plan met vehement opposition from the neighbors.
He made a vehement argument against the merger.
entries.contrast: The stress is on the first syllable and the h is silent: VEE-uh-muhnt. The adverb vehemently (He vehemently denied it) is more common than the adjective.

entries.meaning: Relating to vehicles, especially cars and trucks. ---
examples: The bridge is closed to vehicular traffic.
He was charged with vehicular manslaughter.
Vehicular access is from the alley.
entries.contrast: Formal, mostly traffic and legal language: vehicular traffic, vehicular homicide. In ordinary speech say car or traffic.

entries.meaning: Veiled has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The email contained a thinly veiled threat.
She made a veiled reference to his drinking.
The bride's face was veiled.
The mountains were veiled in fog.

senses.head: Hinted at rather than said openly
examples: The email contained a thinly veiled threat.
She made a veiled reference to his drinking.

senses.head: Covered with a veil or a thin layer
examples: The bride's face was veiled.
The mountains were veiled in fog.

entries.position: both — mostly before a noun in the 'hidden' sense
entries.contrast: Very common in thinly veiled, which means the hint is obvious to everyone: a thinly veiled threat.

entries.meaning: Soft and smooth like velvet — of a texture, a voice or a taste. ---
examples: The petals have a velvety feel.
He has a deep, velvety voice.
The soup was rich and velvety.

entries.meaning: Willing to be bribed; corrupt. ---
examples: The novel is set in a venal city hall.
Reporters exposed a venal inspector who signed off on anything.
The whole system is venal, from top to bottom.
entries.contrast: Don't confuse venal (продажный, берущий взятки) with venial, VEE-nee-uhl, which describes a small, forgivable sin. Formal; everyday English says corrupt or on the take.

entries.meaning: Old and deserving respect. ---
examples: The department is housed in a venerable brick building downtown.
He's a venerable figure in American jazz.
The recipe comes from a venerable family cookbook.

entries.meaning: Passed from person to person through sexual contact. ---
examples: Venereal disease was a taboo subject for decades.
The clinic treats venereal infections free of charge.
The old textbook has a chapter on venereal warts.
entries.contrast: Modern American usage says sexually transmitted instead — an STD, an STI. Venereal now sounds old-fashioned or clinical.

entries.meaning: Belonging to Venice, the city in Italy. ---
examples: We stayed in a Venetian palace that is now a hotel.
The museum owns two Venetian paintings.
Her grandmother was Venetian and never lost the accent.
entries.position: both — always with a capital V
entries.contrast: The window shade is a venetian blind, written with a small v by most American publishers.

entries.meaning: Belonging to Venezuela or its people. ---
examples: Venezuelan oil exports have fallen sharply.
She married a Venezuelan engineer she met in Houston.
The coffee we bought is Venezuelan.
entries.position: both — always with a capital V
entries.contrast: A Venezuelan with a or the is the noun — the person.

entries.meaning: Wanting to punish someone who has hurt you. ---
examples: He came out of prison a bitter, vengeful man.
There was something vengeful in the way she said it.
The hero of the movie is more vengeful than heroic.

entries.meaning: Venomous has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Venomous snakes are common in that part of Texas.
The spider is tiny but venomous.
It's one of the most venomous fish in the world.
She shot him a venomous look across the table.
The email was short and venomous.

senses.head: Producing venom and able to poison with a bite or sting
examples: Venomous snakes are common in that part of Texas.
The spider is tiny but venomous.
It's one of the most venomous fish in the world.

senses.head: Full of bitter hatred
examples: She shot him a venomous look across the table.
The email was short and venomous.

entries.contrast: A venomous animal injects poison when it bites or stings; a poisonous one poisons you if you eat or touch it.

entries.meaning: Supplied with moving fresh air. ---
examples: Use the stain only in a well-ventilated room.
The basement is poorly ventilated and smells of damp.
Store the cans in a cool, ventilated space.
entries.position: both — usually after well or poorly

entries.meaning: Verbal has 2 distinct senses.
examples: We had only a verbal agreement, and now he denies it.
She gave her verbal consent over the phone.
The offer was verbal — nothing was ever signed.
The test measures verbal and math skills separately.
Verbal abuse is still abuse.

senses.head: Spoken rather than written
examples: We had only a verbal agreement, and now he denies it.
She gave her verbal consent over the phone.
The offer was verbal — nothing was ever signed.

senses.head: Having to do with words and the use of language
examples: The test measures verbal and math skills separately.
Verbal abuse is still abuse.

entries.contrast: In a legal context Americans prefer an oral agreement; verbal can also mean simply with words, which is why lawyers avoid it.

entries.meaning: Word for word, exactly as it was said. ---
examples: The paper printed a verbatim transcript of the call.
She gave a verbatim account of the argument.
The quotes in the report are verbatim.
entries.contrast: Also an adverb, with no -ly: he repeated the speech verbatim.

entries.meaning: Using far more words than are needed. ---
examples: The contract is long and verbose.
His writing gets more verbose every year.
Cut the verbose introduction and start with the problem.

entries.meaning: Strictly forbidden. ---
examples: Phones at the dinner table are verboten in our house.
Politics at Thanksgiving is verboten.
Asking what anyone earned was verboten.
entries.position: predicative only — the subject is verboten
entries.contrast: Used half-jokingly, for a rule nobody dares to break. In plain American English say off-limits or forbidden.

entries.meaning: Green with grass and growing plants. ---
examples: The hills were verdant after the spring rains.
They rented a cottage in a verdant valley.
By June the whole yard is verdant.
entries.contrast: A literary word. In everyday speech Americans say green or lush.

entries.meaning: Able to be checked and shown to be true. ---
examples: Give me a verifiable fact, not a rumor.
His account of that night is not verifiable.
Everything on the application has to be verifiable.

entries.meaning: Verified has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The story has not been verified by anyone else.
We need verified numbers before Friday.
He has a verified account on the platform.
Only verified users can post links.

senses.head: Checked and shown to be true
examples: The story has not been verified by anyone else.
We need verified numbers before Friday.

senses.head: Confirmed as genuine by the site that runs the account
examples: He has a verified account on the platform.
Only verified users can post links.

entries.meaning: Used before a noun to say that a strong word really does fit. ---
examples: The kitchen was a veritable disaster area.
He's a veritable encyclopedia of baseball.
The half-price sale drew a veritable mob.
entries.contrast: Veritable only strengthens a comparison you are making; it never means truthful.

entries.meaning: Versatile has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She's the most versatile player on the team.
He's a versatile actor who can do comedy and Shakespeare.
Olive oil is the most versatile thing in my kitchen.
It's a versatile little tool — I use it for everything.

senses.head: Able to do many different things well
examples: She's the most versatile player on the team.
He's a versatile actor who can do comedy and Shakespeare.

senses.head: Useful in many different ways
examples: Olive oil is the most versatile thing in my kitchen.
It's a versatile little tool — I use it for everything.

entries.meaning: Knowing a great deal about a subject. ---
examples: She's well versed in tax law.
You don't have to be versed in music theory to enjoy the concert.
He is more versed in the history of the place than anyone.

entries.meaning: Going straight up and down. ---
examples: Draw a vertical line down the middle of the page.
The cliff face is almost vertical.
The chart uses a vertical axis for price.
entries.contrast: Vertical goes up and down; horizontal goes side to side.

entries.meaning: Vested has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The oil companies have a vested interest in the outcome.
Long-term tenants have a vested right to stay.
You're fully vested after five years.
Her stock options aren't vested yet.

senses.head: Held for good and not to be taken away, said of rights or interests
examples: The oil companies have a vested interest in the outcome.
Long-term tenants have a vested right to stay.

senses.head: Owning your full share of a retirement plan after enough years of service
examples: You're fully vested after five years.
Her stock options aren't vested yet.

entries.position: both — a vested interest before a noun, fully vested after a verb
entries.contrast: A vested interest means a private reason to want one outcome — usually money — not simply an interest in the subject.

entries.meaning: Left over from an earlier stage and no longer of any use. ---
examples: The appendix is a vestigial organ.
Whales still have vestigial hip bones.
The rule is vestigial — nobody has enforced it in years.
entries.form: from vestige — a small trace of something that is gone

entries.meaning: Having done a job for many years. ---
examples: She's a veteran reporter at the paper.
The team signed a veteran pitcher for one more season.
Veteran teachers usually get the harder classes.
entries.contrast: A veteran standing alone is a noun — someone who served in the military.

entries.meaning: Having to do with the medical care of animals. ---
examples: He's studying veterinary medicine at Cornell.
The dog needs veterinary attention tonight.
There's a 24-hour veterinary clinic on Third Street.
entries.contrast: The person is a veterinarian, or a vet for short — veterinary is only the adjective.

entries.meaning: Vexed has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She sounded vexed at the delay.
He was vexed with himself for forgetting the tickets.
Immigration remains a vexed question in both parties.
They came back to the vexed issue of funding.

senses.head: Annoyed and a little upset
examples: She sounded vexed at the delay.
He was vexed with himself for forgetting the tickets.

senses.head: Argued over for years without an answer, said of a question
examples: Immigration remains a vexed question in both parties.
They came back to the vexed issue of funding.

entries.position: both — a vexed question before a noun, vexed at after a verb
entries.takes: at or with + noun; by + noun

entries.meaning: Annoying and hard to settle. ---
examples: It's a vexing problem with no clean answer.
The delays at the border are vexing.
The most vexing part is the paperwork.
entries.contrast: A vexing problem annoys you; a vexed person is the one who is annoyed.

entries.meaning: Viable has 2 distinct senses.
examples: We need a viable plan by Monday.
Solar is now a viable alternative for most homeowners.
That's the only viable option left.
The seeds are still viable after two years in the drawer.
A fetus is generally viable at about 24 weeks.

senses.head: Able to work and succeed
examples: We need a viable plan by Monday.
Solar is now a viable alternative for most homeowners.
That's the only viable option left.

senses.head: Able to live and keep growing
examples: The seeds are still viable after two years in the drawer.
A fetus is generally viable at about 24 weeks.

entries.meaning: Vibrant has 2 distinct senses.
examples: It's a vibrant neighborhood with music every night.
She was eighty and still vibrant.
The walls are a vibrant blue.
Fall colors are more vibrant up north.

senses.head: Full of life and energy
examples: It's a vibrant neighborhood with music every night.
She was eighty and still vibrant.

senses.head: Bright and strong, said of a color
examples: The walls are a vibrant blue.
Fall colors are more vibrant up north.

entries.meaning: Felt by watching someone else do it rather than doing it yourself. ---
examples: Parents get a vicarious thrill out of their kids' wins.
He lives a vicarious life through his brother's travel photos.
The novels gave her vicarious adventure.

entries.meaning: Having to do with a vice president or that office. ---
examples: She's on the short list for the vice-presidential nomination.
The vice-presidential debate is next Tuesday.
He took a vice-presidential post at the bank.

entries.meaning: Vicious has 3 distinct senses.
examples: It was a vicious attack in broad daylight.
The dog is vicious with strangers.
She spread a vicious rumor about him.
The campaign turned vicious in October.
I woke up with a vicious headache.
A vicious storm knocked the power out for three days.

senses.head: Cruel and violent
examples: It was a vicious attack in broad daylight.
The dog is vicious with strangers.

senses.head: Meant to hurt someone with words
examples: She spread a vicious rumor about him.
The campaign turned vicious in October.

senses.head: Very severe or painful
examples: I woke up with a vicious headache.
A vicious storm knocked the power out for three days.

entries.contrast: A vicious circle is one in which each problem makes the next one worse.

entries.meaning: Having won a fight, a game or an election. ---
examples: The team came home victorious.
She was victorious over a field of nine candidates.
The victorious army marched through the square.

entries.meaning: Belonging to Vienna, the capital of Austria. ---
examples: We had coffee in an old Viennese café.
The orchestra played Viennese waltzes all evening.
His accent is unmistakably Viennese.
entries.position: both — always with a capital V

entries.meaning: Able to be watched or seen, usually on a screen. ---
examples: The game is viewable on any device.
The recording stays viewable for thirty days.
Only the first chapter is viewable without an account.

entries.meaning: Watching carefully for danger or trouble. ---
examples: Police asked residents to stay vigilant.
A vigilant neighbor called it in before the fire spread.
You have to be more vigilant about your passwords than that.

entries.meaning: Vigorous has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Thirty minutes of vigorous exercise a day is plenty.
He's seventy and still vigorous.
The mayor made a vigorous defense of the plan.
There was vigorous debate at the meeting.

senses.head: Strong and full of physical energy
examples: Thirty minutes of vigorous exercise a day is plenty.
He's seventy and still vigorous.

senses.head: Done with force and determination
examples: The mayor made a vigorous defense of the plan.
There was vigorous debate at the meeting.

entries.meaning: Vile has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The coffee in that machine tastes vile.
We had three days of vile weather.
It was the vilest thing anyone had ever said to her.
He wrote a vile letter to the family.

senses.head: Extremely unpleasant
examples: The coffee in that machine tastes vile.
We had three days of vile weather.

senses.head: Morally disgusting
examples: It was the vilest thing anyone had ever said to her.
He wrote a vile letter to the family.

entries.meaning: Evil, like the bad character in a story. ---
examples: He plays a villainous banker in the new movie.
It was a villainous thing to do to a friend.
The book gives her a villainous uncle and an empty bank account.

entries.meaning: Shown to have been right all along. ---
examples: She felt vindicated when the report finally came out.
He was fully vindicated by the investigation.
After ten years, the whistleblower was vindicated.

entries.meaning: Wanting to hurt someone who has hurt you. ---
examples: The firing looked petty and vindictive.
He's not cruel, just vindictive when he's been hurt.
She's the most vindictive person I've ever worked with.

entries.meaning: Violent has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He has a history of violent behavior.
Violent crime is down for the third year.
The protest turned violent after midnight.
A violent storm tore through the valley.
She had a violent reaction to the medication.

senses.head: Using physical force to hurt or damage
examples: He has a history of violent behavior.
Violent crime is down for the third year.
The protest turned violent after midnight.

senses.head: Very strong and sudden
examples: A violent storm tore through the valley.
She had a violent reaction to the medication.

entries.meaning: Of a bluish purple color. ---
examples: The sky turned a deep violet after sunset.
She wore a violet scarf with a gray coat.
The petals are pale violet at the edges.
entries.contrast: A violet is also the small flower, and the color is the bluer end of purple.

entries.meaning: Viral has 2 distinct senses.
examples: It's a viral infection, so antibiotics won't help.
The clinic is testing for viral pneumonia.
The video went viral overnight.
They're hoping for a viral hit and a book deal.

senses.head: Caused by a virus
examples: It's a viral infection, so antibiotics won't help.
The clinic is testing for viral pneumonia.

senses.head: Spreading very fast from person to person online
examples: The video went viral overnight.
They're hoping for a viral hit and a book deal.

entries.contrast: Go viral is the fixed phrase for something that spreads fast online.

entries.meaning: Never used, cut or touched before. ---
examples: Loggers moved into the virgin forest in the 1890s.
Use extra virgin olive oil for the salad.
For the company this is virgin territory.
entries.position: attributive only — virgin forest, virgin olive oil
entries.contrast: A virgin meaning a person is a noun; the adjective is about untouched land or first-press oil.

entries.meaning: Strong and manly, in the way a man is traditionally pictured. ---
examples: The ads sell a virile image of the outdoorsman.
He was still virile at sixty.
The part calls for a virile leading man.

entries.meaning: Virtual has 2 distinct senses.
examples: We hold a virtual meeting every Monday morning.
The museum offers a virtual tour of all four floors.
The strike brought the city to a virtual standstill.
He's the virtual head of the company now.

senses.head: Existing on a computer or a network rather than in the real world
examples: We hold a virtual meeting every Monday morning.
The museum offers a virtual tour of all four floors.

senses.head: Almost what you would call it, though not officially so
examples: The strike brought the city to a virtual standstill.
He's the virtual head of the company now.

entries.contrast: The adverb virtually usually means almost — the room was virtually empty.

entries.meaning: Behaving in a morally good way. ---
examples: She led a quiet, virtuous life in a small town.
There's nothing virtuous about doing it for the praise.
He gave me that virtuous look again.
entries.contrast: A virtuous circle is the happy opposite of a vicious circle — each step makes the next one better.

entries.meaning: Virulent has 2 distinct senses.
examples: A virulent strain of the flu hit the region in January.
The infection is more virulent than last year's.
The article set off virulent attacks online.
He is a virulent critic of the new policy.

senses.head: Spreading fast and doing great harm, said of a disease
