entries.meaning: Weary has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The hikers came back cold and weary.
She gave a weary sigh and sat down.
By the third meeting I was wearier than ever.
Voters are weary of the same promises.
I'm weary of hearing about it.

senses.head: Very tired, especially after long effort
examples: The hikers came back cold and weary.
She gave a weary sigh and sat down.
By the third meeting I was wearier than ever.

senses.head: Tired of something because it has gone on too long
examples: Voters are weary of the same promises.
I'm weary of hearing about it.

entries.takes: of + noun or -ing (what you have had too much of)
entries.contrast: Don't mix up weary WEER-ee (tired) with wary WAIR-ee (careful, suspicious): wary of strangers, not weary of strangers.

entries.meaning: Making you very tired. ---
examples: It was a long, wearying drive across the state.
The constant arguing is wearying.
Nothing is more wearying than a day of meetings.
entries.contrast: A wearying trip makes you tired; a weary traveler already is tired.

entries.meaning: Rough and worn from years of sun, wind and rain. ---
examples: A weather-beaten barn stood at the edge of the field.
His face was brown and weather-beaten.
The sign was so weather-beaten you could barely read it.

entries.meaning: Changed in color or texture by long exposure to the weather. ---
examples: The deck is made of gray weathered boards.
Weathered rock shows the layers underneath.
The paint on the shutters looked more weathered than I remembered.
entries.form: -ed from weather (the verb: to change from long exposure)

entries.meaning: Able to stand rain, wind and cold without being damaged. ---
examples: The speakers are weatherproof, so you can leave them outside.
We put a weatherproof cover on the grill.
The new windows are fully weatherproof.

entries.meaning: With skin joining the toes or fingers, as ducks and frogs have. ---
examples: Ducks have webbed feet.
Frogs push through the water with their webbed toes.
The baby was born with slightly webbed fingers.

entries.meaning: Wedded has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Do you take this woman to be your lawfully wedded wife?
They celebrated twenty years of wedded bliss.
The vows speak of a lawfully wedded husband.
The mayor is wedded to the idea of a new stadium.
She's too wedded to her own plan to listen to anyone.

senses.head: Married — formal or legal language
examples: Do you take this woman to be your lawfully wedded wife?
They celebrated twenty years of wedded bliss.
The vows speak of a lawfully wedded husband.

senses.head: So committed to an idea or a method that you will not give it up
examples: The mayor is wedded to the idea of a new stadium.
She's too wedded to her own plan to listen to anyone.

entries.position: both — the 'married' sense before a noun, the 'committed' sense after a verb

entries.meaning: Stuck tightly in a narrow space, so that it is hard to move. ---
examples: The car was wedged between two trucks.
A coin got wedged in the slot.
We sat wedged into the back row of the bus.
entries.position: predicative only — after be, get, sit

entries.meaning: Wee has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Can I have a wee bit of cream in my coffee?
He was just a wee boy when they moved here.
She's a wee thing — barely five feet tall.
We talked until the wee hours of the morning.
The call came in the wee hours of Sunday.

senses.head: Very small — informal and affectionate
examples: Can I have a wee bit of cream in my coffee?
He was just a wee boy when they moved here.
She's a wee thing — barely five feet tall.

senses.head: In the wee hours: the very early hours after midnight
examples: We talked until the wee hours of the morning.
The call came in the wee hours of Sunday.

entries.contrast: Wee came from Scotland and sounds folksy in American English. It is mostly kept for two phrases: a wee bit (чуть-чуть) and the wee hours. For ordinary use say tiny.

entries.meaning: Lasting a week. ---
examples: They went on a weeklong trip to Maine.
The town holds a weeklong festival every August.
A weeklong strike shut down the port.
entries.form: compound — week + long, like daylong, yearlong

entries.meaning: Weeping has 2 distinct senses.
examples: A weeping woman sat on the courthouse steps.
Weeping relatives waited outside the hospital.
There's a weeping willow by the pond.
They planted a weeping cherry in the front yard.

senses.head: Crying
examples: A weeping woman sat on the courthouse steps.
Weeping relatives waited outside the hospital.

senses.head: Of a tree: with long branches that hang down
examples: There's a weeping willow by the pond.
They planted a weeping cherry in the front yard.

entries.contrast: After a verb, weeping is the verb, not the adjective: She was weeping = она плакала. Only before a noun is it an adjective.

entries.meaning: Weepy has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She gets weepy at weddings.
I was tired and weepy by the end of the day.
The kids get weepier the later it gets.
It's a weepy holiday movie.
He put on a weepy love song and ruined the mood.

senses.head: Crying easily, or close to tears
examples: She gets weepy at weddings.
I was tired and weepy by the end of the day.
The kids get weepier the later it gets.

senses.head: Of a movie, a song or a book: sentimental and meant to make you cry
examples: It's a weepy holiday movie.
He put on a weepy love song and ruined the mood.

entries.meaning: Weighed down has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She came in weighed down with grocery bags.
The branches were weighed down by wet snow.
He seemed weighed down by guilt.
The company is weighed down with debt.

senses.head: Carrying so much that it is hard to move
examples: She came in weighed down with grocery bags.
The branches were weighed down by wet snow.

senses.head: Made tired or unhappy by worry, debt or responsibility
examples: He seemed weighed down by guilt.
The company is weighed down with debt.

entries.position: predicative only — after be, feel, seem, come
entries.takes: with or by + noun (what the weight or the worry is)
entries.form: past participle of the phrasal verb weigh down

entries.meaning: Weighted has 3 distinct senses.
examples: She sleeps under a weighted blanket.
The base is weighted so the lamp won't tip over.
Your final grade is a weighted average.
The test is weighted toward the last two chapters.
The rules are weighted in favor of landlords.
The whole system is weighted against small farms.

senses.head: Made heavier by adding weight
examples: She sleeps under a weighted blanket.
The base is weighted so the lamp won't tip over.

senses.head: Counting some parts more than others in a total
examples: Your final grade is a weighted average.
The test is weighted toward the last two chapters.

senses.head: Arranged so that one side has an advantage
examples: The rules are weighted in favor of landlords.
The whole system is weighted against small farms.

entries.русский: утяжелённый; взвешенный (о среднем); смещённый в чью-то пользу
entries.takes: in the 'unfair' sense, toward, in favor of or against + noun

entries.meaning: Having no weight, or feeling as if you have none. ---
examples: Astronauts are weightless in orbit.
The fabric is so light it feels weightless.
For a second at the top of the hill you feel weightless.

entries.meaning: Weighty has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The court has weighty matters to decide this term.
He raised a weightier question than anyone expected.
There are weighty reasons to wait another year.
She carried a weighty volume of poetry under her arm.
The package was weighty enough to need both hands.

senses.head: Serious and important; deserving careful thought
examples: The court has weighty matters to decide this term.
He raised a weightier question than anyone expected.
There are weighty reasons to wait another year.

senses.head: Heavy — a formal or literary use
examples: She carried a weighty volume of poetry under her arm.
The package was weighty enough to need both hands.

entries.meaning: Strange, and hard to explain or get used to. ---
examples: That's a weird thing to say.
It felt weird being back in my old school.
The weirdest part is that nobody noticed.
entries.contrast: Weird breaks the 'i before e' rule — e-i, not i-e. In casual speech people also say weird someone out (to make someone uncomfortable), which is a verb.

entries.meaning: Welcome has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The rain was a welcome change after a month of heat.
Your check was a welcome surprise.
Nothing is more welcome than good news on a Monday.
You're welcome to stay for dinner.
Visitors are welcome in the garden anytime.

senses.head: Gladly received; making people pleased
examples: The rain was a welcome change after a month of heat.
Your check was a welcome surprise.
Nothing is more welcome than good news on a Monday.

senses.head: Allowed and encouraged to do something or take something
examples: You're welcome to stay for dinner.
Visitors are welcome in the garden anytime.

entries.takes: to + noun (something you may take) or a to-infinitive
entries.contrast: You're welcome is the standard answer to thank you. Keep the adjective apart from the verb: Guests are welcome (they are gladly received) but The host welcomed the guests (he greeted them).

entries.meaning: Friendly to visitors and newcomers; making people feel at home. ---
examples: The neighbors were warm and welcoming.
The lobby has a welcoming feel to it.
The church tries hard to be welcoming to newcomers.

entries.meaning: Acting politely and doing what you are told, usually about children or animals. ---
examples: The kids were surprisingly well behaved at dinner.
She runs a well-behaved third-grade class.
Our dog is better behaved than the puppy next door.
entries.position: both — hyphenated before a noun: a well-behaved class; open after a verb: the kids were well behaved
entries.contrast: Comparison uses better and best, not weller: the dog is better behaved than the cat.

entries.meaning: Carefully planned, with the details worked out in advance. ---
examples: It's a well-thought-out plan, and cheap to start.
Her essay was well thought out and clearly written.
This proposal is better thought out than the last one.
entries.position: both — hyphenated before a noun (a well-thought-out plan); written open after a verb
entries.comparison: irregular — better thought out, best thought out
entries.form: compound — well + past participle of think out

entries.meaning: Emotionally healthy and able to deal with other people and with life. ---
examples: They're raising two happy, well-adjusted kids.
He seems well adjusted after everything he's been through.
Children with a steady routine tend to be better adjusted.
entries.position: both — hyphenated before a noun; often written open after a verb
entries.form: compound — well + past participle of adjust

entries.meaning: Sensible or wise to do something. ---
examples: You'd be well-advised to read the contract first.
Drivers would be well-advised to avoid the bridge today.
She'd be well-advised to say nothing until the hearing.
entries.русский: поступающий благоразумно; которому лучше бы (сделать что-то)
entries.position: predicative only — almost always would be well-advised to
entries.contrast: This is a polite, formal way of saying should: You'd be well-advised to call first = вам лучше бы позвонить заранее. Its opposite ill-advised does go before a noun: an ill-advised email.

entries.meaning: Of a room, house or hotel: well furnished and fully equipped — formal. ---
examples: They stayed in a well-appointed suite overlooking the park.
The house is well-appointed, with a wine cellar and a gym.
It's the best-appointed hotel in town.
entries.comparison: irregular — better appointed, best appointed; hyphenated before a noun best-appointed
entries.form: compound — well + appointed, here in the old sense 'furnished, equipped'

entries.meaning: Well-balanced has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Kids need a well-balanced diet.
The team is well balanced on offense and defense.
This year's roster is better balanced than last year's.
She's a well-balanced person who doesn't panic.
He came across as calm and well balanced in the interview.

senses.head: Containing the right mix of different things
examples: Kids need a well-balanced diet.
The team is well balanced on offense and defense.
This year's roster is better balanced than last year's.

senses.head: Of a person: calm, sensible and emotionally steady
examples: She's a well-balanced person who doesn't panic.
He came across as calm and well balanced in the interview.

entries.position: both — hyphenated before a noun; often written open after a verb

entries.meaning: Well-bred has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He's a well-bred young man who writes thank-you notes.
It wouldn't be well-bred to ask what it cost.
The farm sells well-bred quarter horses.
Her dogs are better bred than most of the ones at the show.

senses.head: Polite and well brought up — an older, upper-class word
examples: He's a well-bred young man who writes thank-you notes.
It wouldn't be well-bred to ask what it cost.

senses.head: Of an animal: from good breeding stock
examples: The farm sells well-bred quarter horses.
Her dogs are better bred than most of the ones at the show.

entries.form: compound — well + past participle of breed
entries.contrast: About people, well-bred now sounds old-fashioned and a little snobbish; say polite or well-mannered instead. About animals it is ordinary.

entries.meaning: Picked carefully, and exactly right for the purpose. ---
examples: She thanked them in a few well-chosen words.
The gift was well chosen.
His examples could have been better chosen.

entries.meaning: Well-connected has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Her father is well-connected in Washington.
You need a well-connected lawyer for this.
He's better connected than anyone else on the committee.
The neighborhood is well connected by bus and rail.
They chose a well-connected airport hub.

senses.head: Knowing many important or useful people
examples: Her father is well-connected in Washington.
You need a well-connected lawyer for this.
He's better connected than anyone else on the committee.

senses.head: Of a place: easy to reach by road, rail or flights
examples: The neighborhood is well connected by bus and rail.
They chose a well-connected airport hub.

entries.русский: со связями; с хорошим транспортным сообщением
entries.position: both — hyphenated before a noun; often written open after a verb

entries.meaning: Well-defined has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Each job here has a well-defined set of duties.
The goals need to be better defined before we start.
The role of the committee is well defined in the bylaws.
The border is well defined along the river.
He has well-defined shoulders from years of swimming.

senses.head: Clear and easy to understand, with the limits spelled out
examples: Each job here has a well-defined set of duties.
The goals need to be better defined before we start.
The role of the committee is well defined in the bylaws.

senses.head: With a clear, sharp shape or edge
examples: The border is well defined along the river.
He has well-defined shoulders from years of swimming.

entries.position: both — hyphenated before a noun; often written open after a verb

entries.meaning: Well-done has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He orders his steak well-done.
The burgers came out well done, almost burnt.
How do you like your steak — rare or well-done?
It's a well-done documentary about the flood.
The repair was well done and cost almost nothing.

senses.head: Of meat: cooked all the way through, with no pink inside
examples: He orders his steak well-done.
The burgers came out well done, almost burnt.
How do you like your steak — rare or well-done?

senses.head: Made or carried out skillfully
examples: It's a well-done documentary about the flood.
The repair was well done and cost almost nothing.

entries.comparison: not gradable — of meat the scale is rare, medium rare, medium, medium well, well-done; in the 'done skillfully' sense better done, best done
entries.contrast: Well done! on its own is praise — молодец! As a cooking word, well-done meat has no pink left in it.

entries.meaning: Having had a good, usually long education. ---
examples: She comes from a well-educated family.
The workforce in this county is well educated.
Today's students are better educated than their grandparents were.
entries.position: both — hyphenated before a noun; often written open after a verb

entries.meaning: Having plenty of money or natural resources. ---
examples: The university is well-endowed and can pay for the scholarships.
The region is well endowed with coal and timber.
Private colleges are usually better endowed than state schools.
entries.takes: with + noun (what there is plenty of)
entries.contrast: Said of a person's body, well-endowed is a joking euphemism for large breasts or genitals — keep it for schools, museums and natural resources.

entries.meaning: Getting plenty of good food. ---
examples: The horses looked healthy and well-fed.
A well-fed crowd left the church basement happy.
Children today are better fed than they were a century ago.
entries.position: both — hyphenated before a noun; often written open after a verb

entries.meaning: Based on good reasons or real facts. ---
examples: Their fears turned out to be well-founded.
He had a well-founded suspicion that he was being followed.
My worries were better founded than his.
entries.position: both — hyphenated before a noun; often written open after a verb

entries.meaning: Clean, neat and carefully looked after — of a person's hair and clothes, or of an animal. ---
examples: A well-groomed man in a gray suit answered the door.
Her dog is always well groomed.
He's better groomed now than he was in college.
entries.position: both — hyphenated before a noun; often written open after a verb

entries.meaning: Well-grounded has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The complaint is well-grounded.
Her objection was well grounded in the data.
He's well-grounded in statistics.
Students should be well grounded in the basics before they specialize.
She's better grounded in the theory than the rest of us.

senses.head: Based on solid facts or evidence
examples: The complaint is well-grounded.
Her objection was well grounded in the data.

senses.head: Having a solid basic knowledge of a subject
examples: He's well-grounded in statistics.
Students should be well grounded in the basics before they specialize.
She's better grounded in the theory than the rest of us.

entries.position: both — hyphenated before a noun; often written open after a verb
entries.takes: in the 'trained' sense, in + noun (the subject)

entries.meaning: Having plenty of money. ---
examples: The gallery attracts a well-heeled crowd.
Well-heeled tourists fill the resort every July.
Her clients are the most well-heeled people in the city.

entries.meaning: Knowing a lot about a subject or about what is going on. ---
examples: She's a well-informed reader of the business press.
Voters need to be well informed about the issues.
He's the best-informed person in the room.
entries.position: both — hyphenated before a noun; often written open after a verb
entries.comparison: irregular — better informed, best informed; hyphenated before a noun best-informed

entries.meaning: Meaning to do good, even when the result is not good. ---
examples: It was a well-intentioned rule that made everything slower.
Well-intentioned advice can still hurt.
His comment was well-intentioned but clumsy.
entries.русский: с благими намерениями, из лучших побуждений
entries.contrast: It almost always comes with a but: the intention was good, the result was not. Well-meaning says the same thing about a person.

entries.meaning: Well-kept has 2 distinct senses.
examples: They live in a well-kept house with a big yard.
The gardens are well kept all year.
The trails are better kept on the north side of the park.
That bakery is the city's best-kept secret.
Their engagement was a well-kept secret for months.

senses.head: Looked after carefully; neat and in good condition
examples: They live in a well-kept house with a big yard.
The gardens are well kept all year.
The trails are better kept on the north side of the park.

senses.head: Of a secret: successfully kept from other people
examples: That bakery is the city's best-kept secret.
Their engagement was a well-kept secret for months.

entries.русский: ухоженный, содержащийся в порядке; тщательно хранимый (о секрете)
entries.position: both — hyphenated before a noun; often written open after a verb
entries.comparison: irregular — better kept, best kept; hyphenated before a noun best-kept

entries.meaning: Built carefully and out of good materials. ---
examples: It's an expensive coat, but it's well-made.
The furniture is simple and well made.
These boots are better made than the pair I had before.
entries.position: both — hyphenated before a noun; often written open after a verb

entries.meaning: Polite, with good manners. ---
examples: Their son is quiet and well-mannered.
A well-mannered guest writes a thank-you note.
The dogs are surprisingly well mannered around small kids.
entries.position: both — hyphenated before a noun; often written open after a verb

entries.meaning: Wanting to help, even when the help does not work. ---
examples: A well-meaning neighbor kept bringing casseroles.
Well-meaning people gave us a lot of bad advice.
He's well-meaning, just disorganized.
entries.contrast: Well-meaning describes the person; well-meant describes what was said or done: a well-meaning friend gave me some well-meant advice.

entries.meaning: Of words or an act: intended kindly, though it may not have helped. ---
examples: The advice was well-meant but useless.
Her well-meant remark only made things worse.
I know it was well-meant, so I said thank you.

entries.meaning: Well-preserved has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The town has a well-preserved 18th-century church.
The fossil is remarkably well preserved.
It's the best-preserved Roman theater in the country.
He's seventy and very well-preserved.
She's well preserved for someone who has worked outdoors all her life.

senses.head: Still in good condition after a long time
examples: The town has a well-preserved 18th-century church.
The fossil is remarkably well preserved.
It's the best-preserved Roman theater in the country.

senses.head: Of an older person: still looking young — often said jokingly
examples: He's seventy and very well-preserved.
She's well preserved for someone who has worked outdoors all her life.

entries.position: both — hyphenated before a noun; often written open after a verb
entries.comparison: irregular — better preserved, best preserved; hyphenated before a noun best-preserved

entries.meaning: Having the training and experience that a job needs. ---
examples: We had four well-qualified candidates for the opening.
She's well qualified for the position.
He was the best-qualified applicant by far.
entries.position: both — hyphenated before a noun; often written open after a verb
entries.comparison: irregular — better qualified, best qualified; hyphenated before a noun best-qualified

entries.meaning: Having read a lot of books, and knowing a lot because of it. ---
examples: Her grandfather was a quiet, well-read man.
He's well read in Russian history.
She's better read than anyone I know.
entries.position: both — hyphenated before a noun; often written open after a verb
entries.takes: in + noun (the field you have read about)
entries.contrast: The second part rhymes with bed, not with reed — it is the past participle. Well-read is about the reader; a widely read book is about the book.

entries.meaning: Covering a good range of skills, subjects or experience, not just one. ---
examples: Colleges look for well-rounded applicants.
The program gives students a well-rounded education.
This year's class is better rounded than last year's.
entries.position: both — hyphenated before a noun; often written open after a verb

entries.meaning: Speaking clearly, politely and in an educated way. ---
examples: He's polite and well-spoken.
She was the most well-spoken kid on the debate team.
A well-spoken young woman showed us around the campus.

entries.meaning: Happening at exactly the right moment. ---
examples: His joke was well-timed and broke the tension.
A well-timed phone call saved the deal.
The announcement could hardly have been better timed.
entries.position: both — hyphenated before a noun; often written open after a verb

entries.meaning: Having plenty of money; comfortably rich. ---
examples: They live in a well-to-do suburb north of the city.
Her family was well-to-do but never flashy.
The club draws the more well-to-do residents.
entries.contrast: Well-to-do and well-off mean the same thing; well-to-do sounds a little older and is more often used before a noun.

entries.meaning: Well-worn has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He pulled on a pair of well-worn jeans.
The stone steps are well-worn in the middle.
Her copy of the book is well worn and full of notes.
The speech was full of well-worn phrases.
It's a well-worn argument, but it still works.

senses.head: Used so much that it shows
examples: He pulled on a pair of well-worn jeans.
The stone steps are well-worn in the middle.
Her copy of the book is well worn and full of notes.

senses.head: Of a phrase, a joke or an argument: used too often to be interesting
examples: The speech was full of well-worn phrases.
It's a well-worn argument, but it still works.

entries.position: both — hyphenated before a noun; often written open after a verb

entries.meaning: In, facing, or coming from the west. ---
examples: We rented a place on the west side of town.
A cold west wind blew all afternoon.
The kitchen has a west window that gets the evening sun.
entries.position: attributive only — the west side, a west wind
entries.contrast: Before a noun it is the adjective (west Texas); after a verb west is an adverb (We drove west); the West is a noun. Capitalize it inside names: West Virginia, the West Coast.

entries.meaning: From or relating to the western part of Africa. ---
examples: The restaurant serves West African food.
West African rhythms shaped American blues.
He teaches West African history at the university.
entries.contrast: Both words are capitalized, and there is no hyphen. It is also a noun for a person: She's a West African.

entries.meaning: Traveling toward the west, or leading west. ---
examples: There's a wreck on the westbound side of the highway.
Take the westbound train to Union Station.
All westbound flights were delayed by fog.
entries.русский: идущий на запад, в западном направлении

entries.meaning: Coming from the west, or going toward the west. ---
examples: A steady westerly breeze filled the sails.
The storm is moving in a westerly direction.
They set off on a westerly course toward the islands.
entries.position: attributive only — a westerly wind, a westerly direction
entries.contrast: A westerly wind blows from the west, but a westerly course goes toward the west. It ends in -ly and still is an adjective, not an adverb. The noun the westerlies means the winds themselves.

entries.meaning: Farthest to the west. ---
examples: Alaska has the westernmost point in the United States.
They live in the westernmost county in the state.
The westernmost island is little more than a rock.
entries.comparison: not gradable — the word is already a superlative

entries.meaning: Going or facing toward the west. ---
examples: The class studies the westward expansion of the 1800s.
They made the long westward journey by wagon.
A westward view of the mountains fills the window.
entries.position: attributive only — after a verb the word is the adverb westward
entries.contrast: Before a noun it is an adjective (the westward expansion); after a verb it is an adverb (We drove westward). American English uses westward for both; British English adds -s to the adverb (westwards).

entries.meaning: Having wheels. ---
examples: She rolled in a wheeled suitcase.
The hospital serves meals from wheeled carts.
They loaded the engine onto a wheeled platform.
entries.form: wheel + -ed; also in compounds — four-wheeled, two-wheeled

entries.meaning: Breathing — or running — with a rough whistling sound. ---
examples: The child had a wheezing cough all night.
A wheezing air conditioner rattled in the window.
He answered in a wheezing whisper.

entries.meaning: Whimsical has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The book has whimsical illustrations.
Her house is full of whimsical little details.
The design is more whimsical than practical.
The rules here are whimsical and depend on who's working.
He makes whimsical decisions about who gets promoted.

senses.head: Playful and a little odd, in a charming way
examples: The book has whimsical illustrations.
Her house is full of whimsical little details.
The design is more whimsical than practical.

senses.head: Changing suddenly and for no good reason
examples: The rules here are whimsical and depend on who's working.
He makes whimsical decisions about who gets promoted.

entries.meaning: Complaining in an annoying way, or sounding like it. ---
examples: Don't be so whiny about it.
He has a whiny voice that carries across the office.
The kids get whinier the longer we stay.

entries.meaning: Relating to office work rather than manual work. ---
examples: The city lost thousands of white-collar jobs.
He was convicted of a white-collar crime.
White-collar employees were told to work from home.
entries.form: compound — white + collar, from the white shirts office workers wore

entries.meaning: Having white hair. ---
examples: A white-haired woman waved from the porch.
He's white-haired now, but the voice is the same.
Two white-haired men sat playing chess in the park.
entries.contrast: Russian седой is usually gray-haired if the hair is still partly dark, and white-haired only when it has gone completely white. Note American gray, not British grey.

entries.meaning: White-hot has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The steel comes out of the furnace white-hot.
He watched the white-hot tip of the rod.
She spoke with white-hot anger.
The team is on a white-hot streak.
The debate has reached a white-hot pitch.

senses.head: So hot that the metal glows white
examples: The steel comes out of the furnace white-hot.
He watched the white-hot tip of the rod.

senses.head: Extremely intense — of anger, attention or success
examples: She spoke with white-hot anger.
The team is on a white-hot streak.
The debate has reached a white-hot pitch.

entries.meaning: Requiring the most formal evening dress. ---
examples: It's a white-tie dinner at the embassy.
He rented tails for the white-tie event.
Very few white-tie affairs are left in America.
entries.русский: с самым строгим вечерним дресс-кодом (фрак и белый галстук)
entries.contrast: White-tie is the most formal dress code — tails and a white bow tie; black-tie means a tuxedo and is far more common. Without the hyphen it is a noun: The invitation says white tie.

entries.meaning: Whitewashed has 2 distinct senses.
examples: A whitewashed fence ran along the road.
The cottages are whitewashed every spring.
Critics say the report is whitewashed.
The museum gives a whitewashed version of the town's history.

senses.head: Painted white with a thin mixture of lime and water
examples: A whitewashed fence ran along the road.
The cottages are whitewashed every spring.

senses.head: Cleaned up to hide something shameful
examples: Critics say the report is whitewashed.
The museum gives a whitewashed version of the town's history.

entries.meaning: Whole has 2 distinct senses.
examples: I waited the whole day and nobody called.
She ate the whole pizza by herself.
The whole family came out to the airport.
A snake can swallow an egg whole.
Cook the potatoes whole, then slice them.

senses.head: All of something; entire
examples: I waited the whole day and nobody called.
She ate the whole pizza by herself.
The whole family came out to the airport.

senses.head: In one piece; not cut up or broken
examples: A snake can swallow an egg whole.
Cook the potatoes whole, then slice them.

entries.position: both — the whole day before a noun; swallow it whole after a verb
entries.contrast: Whole comes after the, my, this: my whole life, never whole my life. With plural and uncountable nouns use all: all the students, all the milk, not the whole students. The w is silent — whole sounds like hole (дыра).

entries.meaning: Made with flour that keeps the whole grain. ---
examples: I'd like whole-wheat toast, please.
She only buys whole-wheat pasta.
The recipe calls for a cup of whole-wheat flour.
entries.contrast: Whole-wheat is made from the whole wheat grain; whole-grain is the wider word and covers oats and rye too. British English says wholemeal.

entries.meaning: Complete and sincere, with no doubts held back. ---
examples: The plan has my wholehearted support.
She gave a wholehearted yes.
His approval was wholehearted, which surprised us.

entries.meaning: Wholesale has 2 distinct senses.
examples: We pay the wholesale price.
He runs a wholesale bakery downtown.
Wholesale customers need a tax number.
The fire caused wholesale destruction downtown.
There were wholesale changes in the front office.

senses.head: Relating to selling goods in large amounts to stores rather than to shoppers
examples: We pay the wholesale price.
He runs a wholesale bakery downtown.
Wholesale customers need a tax number.

senses.head: Done on a huge scale, and usually without care
examples: The fire caused wholesale destruction downtown.
There were wholesale changes in the front office.

entries.contrast: Wholesale is also an adverb (They buy wholesale) and a noun. The 'large-scale' sense is nearly always critical: wholesale destruction, wholesale firings.

entries.meaning: Wholesome has 2 distinct senses.
examples: They serve simple, wholesome food.
A wholesome breakfast beats a donut in the car.
Nothing on that menu looked very wholesome.
It's a wholesome family movie.
He has a wholesome, small-town image.
That video is the most wholesome thing on the internet today.

senses.head: Good for your health, especially of food
examples: They serve simple, wholesome food.
A wholesome breakfast beats a donut in the car.
Nothing on that menu looked very wholesome.

senses.head: Morally good and not offensive
examples: It's a wholesome family movie.
He has a wholesome, small-town image.
That video is the most wholesome thing on the internet today.

entries.meaning: Very large — used to stress how big a number or a thing is. ---
examples: The repair cost a whopping twelve hundred dollars.
She won by a whopping thirty points.
He pulled a whopping trout out of the creek.
entries.position: attributive only — usually right before a number: a whopping $40 million

entries.meaning: Wicked has 3 distinct senses.
examples: The wicked stepmother locks her in the tower.
It was a wicked thing to do to an old man.
She plays the wickedest villain on TV.
I've got a wicked headache.
A wicked storm knocked out the power for two days.
They have a wicked sense of humor.
That's a wicked guitar solo.

senses.head: Morally bad; evil — often in stories
examples: The wicked stepmother locks her in the tower.
It was a wicked thing to do to an old man.
She plays the wickedest villain on TV.

senses.head: Very bad, severe or unpleasant
examples: I've got a wicked headache.
A wicked storm knocked out the power for two days.

senses.head: Excellent or impressive — informal praise
examples: They have a wicked sense of humor.
That's a wicked guitar solo.

entries.comparison: -er/-est or more/most — wickeder, wickedest; also more wicked, most wicked
entries.contrast: Two syllables, WIK-id, even though it looks like a past tense. In New England wicked is also an adverb meaning very: It's wicked cold out.

entries.meaning: Of a camera lens or shot: taking in a much wider view than normal. ---
examples: He shot the room with a wide-angle lens.
A wide-angle shot shows the whole stage at once.
The phone has a wide-angle camera on the back.

entries.meaning: Completely awake, not sleepy at all. ---
examples: It was three in the morning and I was wide awake.
The coffee left her wide awake until two.
The baby is wide awake and ready to play.
entries.position: predicative only — usually written open after a verb: I was wide awake

entries.meaning: Wide-eyed has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The kids stood wide-eyed in front of the shark tank.
A wide-eyed toddler watched the parade go by.
He came to the city as a wide-eyed college kid.
She's not the wide-eyed intern she was five years ago.

senses.head: With the eyes wide open in surprise, fear or wonder
examples: The kids stood wide-eyed in front of the shark tank.
A wide-eyed toddler watched the parade go by.

senses.head: Innocent and easily impressed, because you have seen little of the world
examples: He came to the city as a wide-eyed college kid.
She's not the wide-eyed intern she was five years ago.

entries.meaning: Wide-open has 3 distinct senses.
examples: He left the front door wide open.
The wide-open windows let in all the noise from the street.
The race for governor is wide open.
It's a wide-open market — anyone can sell there.
They moved west for the wide-open spaces.
The highway runs for hours through wide-open country.

senses.head: Open as far as it will go
examples: He left the front door wide open.
The wide-open windows let in all the noise from the street.

senses.head: With no clear winner yet, or with no limits
examples: The race for governor is wide open.
It's a wide-open market — anyone can sell there.

senses.head: Of land: flat, empty and stretching a long way
examples: They moved west for the wide-open spaces.
The highway runs for hours through wide-open country.

entries.русский: распахнутый; с непредсказуемым исходом; открытый, просторный
entries.position: both — hyphenated before a noun (a wide-open field); written open after a verb (the door was wide open)

entries.meaning: Covering many different subjects, or a large area. ---
examples: They had a wide-ranging conversation about politics and art.
The bill makes wide-ranging changes to the tax code.
Her interests are wide-ranging, from opera to baseball.

entries.meaning: Made for, or having, a screen that is much wider than it is tall. ---
examples: The movie was shot in wide-screen format.
He bought a wide-screen TV for the basement.
The wide-screen version keeps the whole picture.
entries.contrast: Americans now usually write it as one word: a widescreen TV.

entries.meaning: Happening or found over a large area, or among many people. ---
examples: The storm caused widespread flooding.
There is widespread support for the new library.
The practice is more widespread than people think.

entries.meaning: Having lost a husband or a wife, and not married again. ---
examples: He moved in with his widowed mother.
She was widowed at forty and raised three kids alone.
The program helps widowed seniors stay in their homes.

entries.meaning: Wild has 4 distinct senses.
examples: Wild horses still roam these hills.
We picked wild blackberries along the fence.
The wildest parts of the state have no roads at all.
The crowd went wild when the band came out.
It was a wild party, and the neighbors called the police.
The wind got wilder after midnight.
The kids are wild about the new dog.
I'm not wild about the color, to be honest.
That's a wild guess, but it's close.
The rumor is wild speculation and nothing more.

senses.head: Living or growing in nature; not kept or planted by people
examples: Wild horses still roam these hills.
We picked wild blackberries along the fence.
The wildest parts of the state have no roads at all.

senses.head: Not controlled; noisy, crazy or violent
examples: The crowd went wild when the band came out.
It was a wild party, and the neighbors called the police.
The wind got wilder after midnight.

senses.head: Very enthusiastic about something
examples: The kids are wild about the new dog.
I'm not wild about the color, to be honest.

senses.head: Not based on facts; random
examples: That's a wild guess, but it's close.
The rumor is wild speculation and nothing more.

entries.takes: in the 'enthusiastic' sense, about + noun or -ing
entries.contrast: In the wild (в дикой природе) is a noun phrase, and wildly is the adverb: He guessed wildly.

entries.meaning: Wild-eyed has 2 distinct senses.
examples: A wild-eyed man burst into the diner.
She came home wild-eyed and out of breath.
Nobody would fund his wild-eyed scheme.
The article dismisses the whole thing as wild-eyed nonsense.

senses.head: Looking shocked, frightened or half crazy
examples: A wild-eyed man burst into the diner.
She came home wild-eyed and out of breath.

senses.head: Of a plan or an idea: extreme and completely unrealistic
examples: Nobody would fund his wild-eyed scheme.
The article dismisses the whole thing as wild-eyed nonsense.

entries.meaning: Willful has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The judge called it a willful violation of the order.
Willful ignorance is no excuse.
They were fined for willful damage to public property.
She was a willful child who never took no for an answer.
He's too willful to follow anyone else's plan.

senses.head: Done on purpose — almost always of something bad
examples: The judge called it a willful violation of the order.
Willful ignorance is no excuse.
They were fined for willful damage to public property.

senses.head: Determined to do what you want, whatever anyone says
examples: She was a willful child who never took no for an answer.
He's too willful to follow anyone else's plan.

entries.contrast: American spelling willful, British wilful with one l. In legal English it means 'done on purpose': willful misconduct.

entries.meaning: Tall, slim and graceful. ---
examples: A willowy dancer crossed the stage.
She's willowy and quiet, and easy to miss in a crowd.
He remembered her as a willowy teenager in a summer dress.
entries.form: -y from willow, the tree with long thin branches

entries.meaning: Wilted has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She threw out the wilted tulips.
The lettuce in the fridge is wilted.
A few wilted plants sat on the windowsill.
Serve the steak over wilted spinach.
The salad comes with wilted greens and bacon.

senses.head: Of a plant or flower: drooping, usually from lack of water
examples: She threw out the wilted tulips.
The lettuce in the fridge is wilted.
A few wilted plants sat on the windowsill.

senses.head: Of greens: cooked just long enough to go soft
examples: Serve the steak over wilted spinach.
The salad comes with wilted greens and bacon.

entries.meaning: Clever at getting what you want, usually by tricks. ---
examples: The wily old lawyer had one more move left.
Coyotes are wily enough to live in the suburbs.
He's the wiliest negotiator in the building.
entries.form: -y from the old noun wile (a trick)

entries.meaning: Weak, or without the nerve to do something — said with mild contempt. ---
examples: Don't be wimpy — just tell her what you think.
He made some wimpy excuse and left early.
The coffee here is wimpier than the stuff at the diner.

entries.meaning: Messy or bent out of shape by the wind. ---
examples: She came in with windblown hair and red cheeks.
The pines along the cliff are low and windblown.
His windblown look takes twenty minutes in front of the mirror.

entries.meaning: Out of breath after effort or a blow. ---
examples: I was completely winded after the third flight of stairs.
He gets winded just carrying the groceries in.
The tackle left her winded but not hurt.
entries.position: predicative only — after a verb: I was winded
entries.contrast: Winded (out of breath) is /ˈwɪndɪd/. The verb wind meaning to turn is /waɪnd/, and its participle wound /waʊnd/ is a different word again.

entries.meaning: Turning first one way and then the other instead of running straight. ---
examples: We took a winding road through the hills.
A long, winding staircase led up to the tower.
The path is narrow and winding, so drive slowly.
entries.contrast: Say /ˈwaɪndɪŋ/, with the vowel of find. The weather word windy is /ˈwɪndi/.

entries.meaning: Windswept has 2 distinct senses.
examples: They got married on a windswept beach in Maine.
The windswept plains go on for hundreds of miles.
It is a beautiful house, but the yard is cold and windswept.
She pushed her windswept hair out of her face.
He showed up half an hour late and thoroughly windswept.

senses.head: Open to the wind, with nothing to block it
examples: They got married on a windswept beach in Maine.
The windswept plains go on for hundreds of miles.
It is a beautiful house, but the yard is cold and windswept.

senses.head: Blown out of place by the wind
examples: She pushed her windswept hair out of her face.
He showed up half an hour late and thoroughly windswept.

entries.meaning: Worked by a spring that you turn with a key or a handle. ---
examples: The baby loves that little windup penguin.
He collects old windup clocks.
It is a windup flashlight, so you never need batteries.
entries.position: attributive only — before a noun: a windup toy
entries.form: compound — from the phrasal verb wind up
entries.contrast: Also written wind-up. The noun windup is the pitcher's motion in baseball.

entries.meaning: With a lot of wind blowing. ---
examples: It is cold and windy out there — take a jacket.
Chicago is windier than people expect in the spring.
We picked the windiest day of the year to go sailing.

entries.meaning: Having wings. ---
examples: Ants produce winged forms once a year.
A winged statue stands over the entrance.
Winged seeds spin down from the maple in May.
entries.position: attributive only — before a noun: a winged insect
entries.contrast: In poetry and in a few fixed phrases it has two syllables: /ˈwɪŋɪd/.

entries.meaning: Without a single win. ---
examples: The team is still winless after nine games.
They ended a winless season by firing the coach.
He is winless in his last twelve starts.

entries.meaning: Winning has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She scored the winning goal in the last minute.
Here are tonight's winning numbers.
The winning team goes to the finals.
He has a winning smile and he knows it.
Her winning manner got them through the door.

senses.head: That wins, or that has won
examples: She scored the winning goal in the last minute.
Here are tonight's winning numbers.
The winning team goes to the finals.

senses.head: Charming in a way that makes people like you right away
examples: He has a winning smile and he knows it.
Her winning manner got them through the door.

entries.position: attributive only — before a noun: the winning goal
entries.comparison: more/most — more winning, most winning — only in the 'charming' sense
entries.contrast: Before a noun it is an adjective; in we are winning it is part of the verb.

entries.meaning: Attractive in a simple, cheerful way. ---
examples: A winsome kid with a gap-toothed grin answered the door.
The movie has a winsome lead and not much else.
She was winsome on camera and tough in the meeting.
entries.form: -some — from an old word for joy, not from win
entries.contrast: Slightly literary. Charming or appealing is the everyday word.

entries.meaning: Wintry has 2 distinct senses.
examples: A wintry mix of rain and snow is on the way.
It felt wintrier than usual for early October.
We drove home under a low, wintry sky.
She gave him a wintry smile and kept walking.
His answer was polite but wintry.

senses.head: Cold and gray, the way winter is
examples: A wintry mix of rain and snow is on the way.
It felt wintrier than usual for early October.
We drove home under a low, wintry sky.

senses.head: Cold and unfriendly
examples: She gave him a wintry smile and kept walking.
His answer was polite but wintry.

entries.comparison: -er/-est or more/most — wintrier, wintriest, more wintry

entries.meaning: Completely exhausted. ---
examples: I'm wiped out — I'm going to bed.
The kids were wiped out after the water park.
She sounded wiped out on the phone.
entries.position: predicative only — after a verb: I'm wiped out
entries.comparison: more/most — more wiped out, most wiped out
entries.form: compound — from the phrasal verb wipe out
entries.contrast: The same words serve as the passive of the verb (the storm wiped out the crop); the adjective is the 'exhausted' one, and it never goes before a noun.

entries.meaning: Wired has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Three cups of coffee and I'm totally wired.
The kids are wired from all that sugar.
He was still wired an hour after the game.
Every room in the building is wired for internet.
The house was wired in 1954 and needs an update.

senses.head: Too keyed up to settle down, often from caffeine
examples: Three cups of coffee and I'm totally wired.
The kids are wired from all that sugar.
He was still wired an hour after the game.

senses.head: Fitted with wiring, or connected to a network
examples: Every room in the building is wired for internet.
The house was wired in 1954 and needs an update.

entries.meaning: Working without a cable. ---
examples: We finally got a wireless printer.
The keyboard is wireless, so there is no cable to trip over.
Ask the front desk for the wireless password.

entries.meaning: Wiry has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He is wiry — all muscle and no weight.
A wiry little terrier came running down the hall.
The climbers were wirier than any of us expected.
She has thick, wiry hair.
The dog has a wiry coat that never lies flat.

senses.head: Thin but strong
examples: He is wiry — all muscle and no weight.
A wiry little terrier came running down the hall.
The climbers were wirier than any of us expected.

senses.head: Stiff and springy, like wire
examples: She has thick, wiry hair.
The dog has a wiry coat that never lies flat.

entries.meaning: Based on what you hope for rather than on the facts. ---
examples: Saying the deal will close by Friday is wishful thinking.
That is a nice plan, but it is mostly wishful thinking.
A little wishful thinking never hurt anybody.
entries.position: attributive only — almost always in wishful thinking
entries.contrast: Practically a one-phrase word: wishful thinking. You cannot say I was wishful.

entries.meaning: Weak and undecided, without a clear position. ---
examples: He gave a wishy-washy answer that satisfied nobody.
Don't be so wishy-washy — pick a restaurant.
The report's conclusion is wishy-washy on purpose.
entries.form: compound — a rhyming double of washy, watered down

entries.meaning: Thin, light and not thick enough to hold together. ---
examples: Wispy clouds hung over the lake.
He has a wispy little beard.
Her hair is finer and wispier than it used to be.

entries.meaning: Quietly sad about something you miss or cannot have. ---
examples: She sounded wistful about her old neighborhood.
He gave the house one last, wistful look.
There is a wistful tone to the whole album.

entries.meaning: Quiet and closed off, not wanting to be with people. ---
examples: He has been quiet and withdrawn since the move.
She became more withdrawn after her sister left.
Teachers noticed a withdrawn, silent kid in the back row.

entries.meaning: Dried up and shrunken from age or lack of water. ---
examples: The plants on the porch were brown and withered.
A few withered apples still hung on the tree.
His withered left hand never fully recovered.

entries.meaning: So scornful or harsh that it crushes the person it is aimed at. ---
examples: She shot him a withering look across the table.
The senator faced withering criticism from her own party.
His response was brief and withering.
entries.contrast: Here it means crushing, not drying up. The plant meaning stays with the verb: the flowers are withering.

entries.meaning: Funny in a quick, clever way. ---
examples: She is the wittiest person in the room, every time.
He wrote a short, witty thank-you note.
The dialogue is witty without trying too hard.

entries.meaning: Small, dry and lined with age. ---
examples: A wizened old man sold tickets at the door.
Her hands were small and wizened.
Wizened apples sat in a bowl by the window.
entries.contrast: Two syllables: /ˈwɪzənd/, with the vowel of wizard.

entries.meaning: Moving from side to side instead of staying steady. ---
examples: This table is wobbly — put something under the leg.
My legs felt wobbly after the flu.
The back wheel got wobblier with every mile.

entries.meaning: Woeful has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The team's defense was woeful all season.
There is a woeful lack of parking downtown.
His Spanish is woeful, but he keeps trying.
She told the whole woeful story over coffee.
The dog gave me a woeful look from the doorway.

senses.head: Bad enough to be embarrassing
examples: The team's defense was woeful all season.
There is a woeful lack of parking downtown.
His Spanish is woeful, but he keeps trying.

senses.head: Full of sadness
examples: She told the whole woeful story over coffee.
The dog gave me a woeful look from the doorway.

entries.meaning: Having the qualities or the shape thought of as a grown woman's. ---
examples: She had a calm, womanly authority in the room.
The dress was cut to show a womanly shape.
He praised what he called her womanly patience — she was not flattered.
entries.form: -ly from woman — an adjective, not an adverb
entries.contrast: An -ly word that is an adjective: a womanly figure, never she smiled womanly. Compare womanish, which is an insult.

entries.meaning: Extremely good or pleasant. ---
examples: We had a wonderful time in Vermont.
That smells wonderful — what is it?
She has been absolutely wonderful about the whole thing.
entries.contrast: Already a strong word, so very wonderful sounds odd; say absolutely wonderful.

entries.meaning: Strange and beautiful enough to make you wonder at it. ---
examples: The canyon at sunrise is a wondrous sight.
He told wondrous stories about his years at sea.
The exhibit is full of wondrous little machines.
entries.contrast: Literary or half-joking in modern American English; wonderful or amazing is the everyday word.

entries.meaning: Wonky has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The shelf is a little wonky on the left.

The app gets wonkier with every update.
It is a wonky piece about tax credits.
The conversation got wonky fast.

senses.head: Crooked, shaky or not working right — informal
examples: The shelf is a little wonky on the left.
My knee has been wonky since the hike.
The app gets wonkier with every update.

senses.head: Full of technical detail, the way a policy expert talks
examples: It is a wonky piece about tax credits.
The conversation got wonky fast.

entries.form: -y — the policy sense is from wonk, a detail-obsessed expert

entries.meaning: Burning wood as fuel. ---
examples: They put a wood-burning stove in the cabin.
The house has a wood-burning fireplace.
Wood-burning heaters are banned on high-pollution days.
entries.position: attributive only — before a noun: a wood-burning stove

entries.meaning: Heated by a wood fire, said of ovens, grills and what comes out of them. ---
examples: They bake everything in a wood-fired oven.
We split a wood-fired pizza and a salad.
The restaurant's wood-fired grill runs all day.
entries.position: attributive only — before a noun: a wood-fired oven

entries.meaning: Covered with trees. ---
examples: The trail runs through a wooded valley.
They bought a wooded lot outside of town.
The north side of the island is more heavily wooded.

entries.meaning: Woody has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The wine has a woody finish.
Older asparagus goes woody at the bottom.
The candle has a warm, woody smell.
A woody hillside rises behind the house.
We camped in a woodier part of the park.

senses.head: Like wood in smell, taste or texture
examples: The wine has a woody finish.
Older asparagus goes woody at the bottom.
The candle has a warm, woody smell.

senses.head: Covered with trees
examples: A woody hillside rises behind the house.
We camped in a woodier part of the park.

entries.meaning: Woolly has 2 distinct senses.

The puppy still has its woolly undercoat.

The argument goes woolly in the middle.
That is woolly thinking, not a plan.

senses.head: Made of wool, or thick and soft like wool
examples: He pulled on a woolly hat and gloves.
The puppy still has its woolly undercoat.
That old blanket is the woolliest thing in the house.

senses.head: Vague and badly organized, of thinking or writing
examples: The argument goes woolly in the middle.
That is woolly thinking, not a plan.

entries.contrast: Woolly keeps both l's, but the related adjective is woolen in American English and woollen in British.

entries.meaning: Dizzy and slightly sick. ---
examples: I felt woozy when I stood up too fast.

He got woozier as the heat went up.

entries.meaning: Spread by people telling each other rather than by advertising. ---
examples: The band built its audience on word-of-mouth buzz.
Word-of-mouth recommendations beat every ad we ran.
It was a word-of-mouth hit before the reviews came out.
entries.русский: из уст в уста, по сарафанному радио
entries.position: attributive only — before a noun: word-of-mouth advertising
entries.form: compound — from the phrase by word of mouth
entries.contrast: Hyphens before a noun. After a verb use the noun phrase instead: the restaurant grew by word of mouth.

entries.meaning: Without any words spoken. ---
examples: They exchanged a wordless look and got up.
The film ends with a long, wordless scene.
He answered with a wordless shrug.

entries.meaning: Using more words than it needs. ---
examples: The contract is wordy and hard to follow.

Cut the wordiest paragraphs first.

entries.meaning: Good enough to be put into practice. ---
examples: We finally have a workable plan.

entries.meaning: Upset or excited about something, usually more than it deserves. ---
examples: Don't get worked up about something that has not happened.

entries.position: predicative only — after a verb: don't get worked up
entries.comparison: more/most — more worked up, most worked up
entries.form: compound — from the phrasal verb work up

entries.meaning: Working has 3 distinct senses.

I have a working knowledge of Spanish.
The working title was 'The Long Way Home.'
That is our working assumption until we hear otherwise.

senses.head: Having a paid job
examples: Day care is expensive for working parents.
Most of our students are working adults.
She has been a working musician since she was nineteen.

senses.head: In operation, not broken
examples: Is there a working bathroom on this floor?
The museum has a working model of the mill.
We need a working phone number for the file.

senses.head: Good enough to go on with for now
examples: I have a working knowledge of Spanish.
The working title was 'The Long Way Home.'
That is our working assumption until we hear otherwise.

entries.position: attributive only — before a noun: a working mother
entries.contrast: Only before a noun. After a verb, is working is the verb: the elevator is working again.

entries.meaning: Belonging to the part of society that does manual or hourly work. ---
examples: He grew up in a working-class neighborhood in Cleveland.
Her family is working-class and proud of it.
The movie is about working-class kids in the 1970s.
entries.form: compound — the noun phrase working class used as an adjective
entries.contrast: Hyphenated as an adjective (a working-class neighborhood); the noun phrase is two words (the working class).

entries.meaning: As good as the best anywhere in the world. ---
examples: The hospital has a world-class cancer center.
She is a world-class cellist.
The food is good, but it is not world-class.

entries.meaning: Tired of life, having seen too much of it to be surprised by anything. ---
examples: He plays a world-weary detective with a bad knee.
She sounded world-weary for someone of twenty-five.
There is a world-weary humor running through his writing.

entries.meaning: Happening or existing everywhere in the world. ---
examples: The company has worldwide distribution.
It became a worldwide phenomenon overnight.
Demand is worldwide, not just here.
entries.contrast: The same word is also an adverb: the book sold two million copies worldwide.

entries.meaning: Worn has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The carpet is worn in front of the door.
He wore a worn leather jacket and no hat.
These tires are more worn than they look.
Her face looked worn after the night shift.
He seemed thin and worn when we saw him in May.

senses.head: Damaged or made thin by long use
examples: The carpet is worn in front of the door.
He wore a worn leather jacket and no hat.
These tires are more worn than they look.

senses.head: Looking tired and used up
examples: Her face looked worn after the night shift.
He seemed thin and worn when we saw him in May.

entries.meaning: Worn-out has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He finally threw out his worn-out sneakers.
A worn-out couch sat by the curb all week.
The engine parts are worn out and need replacing.
I'm worn out from the drive.
The nurses are worn out and short-staffed.

senses.head: Too old or damaged to be used any longer
examples: He finally threw out his worn-out sneakers.
A worn-out couch sat by the curb all week.
The engine parts are worn out and need replacing.

senses.head: Completely exhausted
examples: I'm worn out from the drive.
The nurses are worn out and short-staffed.

entries.form: compound — from the phrasal verb wear out
entries.contrast: Hyphen before a noun (worn-out shoes); after a verb most Americans write it as two words: I'm worn out.

entries.meaning: Giving you reason to worry. ---
examples: The test results are worrisome but not conclusive.
There is a worrisome crack in the ceiling.
The most worrisome part is how fast it spread.
entries.contrast: Americans say worrisome; the British usually say worrying.

entries.meaning: Getting worse as time goes on. ---
examples: Worsening weather forced them to turn back.
Doctors pointed to his worsening symptoms.
The report describes a worsening housing shortage.
entries.position: attributive only — before a noun: worsening weather

entries.meaning: Worthless has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The stock turned out to be worthless.
Without the receipt the warranty is worthless.
He inherited a box of worthless old bonds.
Depression can make you feel worthless.
His father called him worthless one too many times.

senses.head: Having no value at all
examples: The stock turned out to be worthless.
Without the receipt the warranty is worthless.
He inherited a box of worthless old bonds.

senses.head: Good for nothing — of a person
examples: Depression can make you feel worthless.
His father called him worthless one too many times.

entries.meaning: Worth the time, money or trouble it costs. ---
examples: It is a long drive, but the museum is worthwhile.
We made a few worthwhile changes to the draft.
It is worthwhile to call ahead and check.
entries.contrast: Worthwhile is one word and needs no preposition. Worth takes a noun or -ing straight after it: worth the money, worth doing.

entries.meaning: Hoping or trying to be the thing named. ---
examples: The city is full of would-be screenwriters.
A would-be thief got stuck in the window.
She gives advice to would-be founders.
entries.position: attributive only — before a noun: a would-be writer
entries.contrast: It marks someone trying or hoping to be something, usually with a hint that they have not managed it: a would-be actor has not made it yet.

entries.meaning: Tense and excited, unable to relax. ---
examples: He was too wound up to sleep.
She gets wound up about deadlines.
The kids are all wound up tonight.
entries.position: predicative only — after a verb: he was wound up
entries.comparison: more/most — more wound up, most wound up
entries.form: compound — from the phrasal verb wind up
entries.contrast: Here wound rhymes with found. The noun wound (an injury) is /wuːnd/ and is a different word.

entries.meaning: Made by crossing threads or strips over and under each other. ---
examples: A woven basket sat by the fireplace.
The chair has a woven cane seat.
She brought back a hand-woven rug from Oaxaca.

entries.meaning: Covered in paper, cloth or plastic. ---
examples: The sandwiches are wrapped and in the fridge.
She handed me a small, wrapped box.
The statue stayed wrapped in plastic all winter.
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like rapt, which means completely absorbed: a rapt audience.

entries.meaning: Wrapped up has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He is completely wrapped up in his own problems.
She was so wrapped up in the book that she missed her stop.
They are too wrapped up in each other to notice.
Everything is wrapped up — we can go home.
With the paperwork wrapped up, we finally relaxed.

senses.head: So absorbed in something that you notice nothing else
examples: He is completely wrapped up in his own problems.
She was so wrapped up in the book that she missed her stop.
They are too wrapped up in each other to notice.

senses.head: Finished and settled
examples: Everything is wrapped up — we can go home.
With the paperwork wrapped up, we finally relaxed.

entries.position: predicative only — after a verb: she's wrapped up in work
entries.comparison: more/most — more wrapped up, most wrapped up
entries.form: compound — from the phrasal verb wrap up

entries.meaning: Wrecked has 2 distinct senses.
examples: A wrecked car sat in the driveway for months.
They photographed the wrecked buildings from the air.
Divers found the wrecked fishing boat in forty feet of water.
I was wrecked after the red-eye.
She is wrecked by the time the kids go to bed.

senses.head: Badly damaged or destroyed
examples: A wrecked car sat in the driveway for months.
They photographed the wrecked buildings from the air.
Divers found the wrecked fishing boat in forty feet of water.

senses.head: Completely exhausted — informal
examples: I was wrecked after the red-eye.
She is wrecked by the time the kids go to bed.

entries.meaning: Causing sharp emotional pain. ---
examples: It was a wrenching decision to sell the farm.
The last chapter is wrenching.
They made a wrenching documentary about the flood.
entries.form: from the verb wrench; often in gut-wrenching, heart-wrenching

entries.meaning: Wretched has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He felt wretched about the way he had spoken to her.
The families lived in wretched conditions all winter.
I had the flu and felt absolutely wretched.
The service was wretched and the food was worse.
We sat through a wretched second half.

senses.head: Very unhappy, or living in miserable conditions
examples: He felt wretched about the way he had spoken to her.
The families lived in wretched conditions all winter.
I had the flu and felt absolutely wretched.

senses.head: Very bad in quality
examples: The service was wretched and the food was worse.
We sat through a wretched second half.

entries.contrast: The -ed is a full syllable: /ˈrɛtʃɪd/, like naked and wicked.

entries.meaning: Wrinkled has 2 distinct senses.
examples: His shirt was wrinkled from the suitcase.
She smoothed out a wrinkled receipt on the counter.
Linen looks wrinkled no matter what you do.
His hands were brown and wrinkled.
A wrinkled face broke into a grin.

senses.head: Full of creases, of cloth or paper
examples: His shirt was wrinkled from the suitcase.
She smoothed out a wrinkled receipt on the counter.
Linen looks wrinkled no matter what you do.

senses.head: Lined with age, of skin
examples: His hands were brown and wrinkled.
A wrinkled face broke into a grin.

entries.meaning: Covered in small folds or creases. ---
examples: The puppy has wrinkly little legs.
My fingers got wrinkly in the bath.
This shirt is even wrinklier than the last one.
entries.contrast: Wrinkly describes how something looks; wrinkled says what happened to it.

entries.meaning: Put down in writing rather than spoken. ---
examples: You need written permission from a parent.
There is a written test and a road test.
Their written English is better than their speaking.
entries.position: attributive only — before a noun: written permission
entries.contrast: Only before a noun in this sense. After a verb, is written is the verb: the rule is written down somewhere.

entries.meaning: Done unfairly or against the law. ---
examples: She sued the company for wrongful termination.
The family filed a wrongful death claim.
He spent nine years in prison after a wrongful conviction.
entries.position: attributive only — before a noun: wrongful termination
entries.contrast: A legal word: wrongful death, wrongful termination, wrongful conviction. For everyday wrongness use wrong.

entries.meaning: Based on stubbornly bad judgment. ---
examples: The whole policy is wrongheaded.
That is a wrongheaded way to read the data.
Cutting the budget now would be wrongheaded.
entries.contrast: Also written wrong-headed. It attacks the thinking behind a decision, not just the result.

entries.meaning: Wry has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He has a wry sense of humor about getting older.
Her wry commentary is the best part of the show.
The book is sad and wry at the same time.
She gave a wry smile and shook her head.
He made a wry face at the first sip.

senses.head: Dryly funny about something that is not really funny
examples: He has a wry sense of humor about getting older.
Her wry commentary is the best part of the show.
The book is sad and wry at the same time.

senses.head: Twisted a little to one side, showing amusement or distaste
examples: She gave a wry smile and shook her head.
He made a wry face at the first sip.

entries.meaning: Hostile toward foreigners. ---
examples: The party's platform got more xenophobic every year.
He apologized for a xenophobic remark.
The campaign ran an openly xenophobic ad.

entries.meaning: Of the northern United States, especially New England. ---
examples: He liked to talk about Yankee ingenuity.
She kept the Yankee habit of saving everything.
The book follows Yankee traders across the Pacific.
entries.position: attributive only — before a noun: Yankee ingenuity
entries.contrast: Inside the US it means a New Englander or a Northerner; outside it means any American. Always capitalized, and most often a noun (a Yankee).

entries.meaning: Wide open, of a gap, a hole or a difference. ---
examples: There is a yawning gap between the two offers.
A yawning hole opened in the street.
The report points to a yawning skills shortage.
entries.position: attributive only — before a noun: a yawning gap
entries.contrast: In this sense it means wide open, not sleepy. A yawning student is simply one who is yawning.

entries.meaning: Happening at or covering the end of the year. ---
examples: The year-end report goes out in January.
She got a nice year-end bonus.
Year-end sales cleared out the old stock.
entries.position: attributive only — before a noun: the year-end report

entries.meaning: Going on through all four seasons. ---
examples: The district moved to a year-round school calendar.
It is a year-round resort, not just a ski town.
They need year-round staff, not seasonal help.
entries.position: attributive only — before a noun: a year-round school
entries.contrast: The same word is an adverb after the verb: the pool is open year-round.

entries.meaning: Lasting a whole year. ---
examples: She is on a yearlong leave from the university.
The museum is closing for a yearlong renovation.
It was a yearlong study of four hundred families.
entries.position: attributive only — before a noun: a yearlong study

entries.meaning: Turned yellow with age. ---
examples: He kept a box of yellowed newspaper clippings.
The pages are yellowed and brittle.
Yellowed lace curtains hung in the front window.
entries.form: from the verb yellow — turned yellow with age

entries.meaning: Slightly yellow. ---
examples: The walls are a yellowish white.
The light in the hallway is yellowish and dim.
It leaves a yellowish stain on the fabric.

entries.meaning: From Yemen, or having to do with Yemen. ---
examples: We ate at a Yemeni restaurant in Dearborn.
Yemeni coffee is famous.
Her husband is Yemeni.
entries.contrast: Also a noun for the person: a Yemeni, two Yemenis. Always capitalized.

entries.meaning: Young in the way you look or act, or belonging to a person's young years. ---
examples: She has a youthful energy that wears the rest of us out.
He apologized for his youthful mistakes.
At seventy he still looks youthful.
entries.contrast: Youthful means young-seeming or typical of young people; young is the plain fact of age. A sixty-year-old can look youthful but is not young.

entries.meaning: Disgusting, especially to taste or touch. ---
examples: There is something yucky in the bottom of the sink.
The medicine tastes yucky.
This is the yuckiest one in the whole box.
entries.contrast: A child's word — fine at the kitchen table, out of place in writing.

entries.meaning: From the former Yugoslavia, or having to do with it. ---
examples: His parents came over on a Yugoslav passport.
The museum has a room of Yugoslav film posters.
She studies the Yugoslav economy of the 1970s.
entries.contrast: Historical: Yugoslavia broke up in the 1990s. For today's countries say Serbian, Croatian, Bosnian or Slovenian. Yugoslavian is the other adjective form.

entries.meaning: Very good to eat. ---
examples: Something yummy is coming out of the oven.
These are even yummier with chocolate chips.
The soup was yummy, thanks.
entries.contrast: Casual and a little childlike; in writing use delicious.

entries.meaning: From Zambia, or having to do with Zambia. ---
examples: The Zambian team qualified for the final.
He teaches Zambian history.
Her mother is Zambian.
entries.contrast: Also a noun for the person: a Zambian. Always capitalized.

entries.meaning: Funny in a silly, unpredictable way. ---
examples: It is a zany comedy about a family road trip.
He has a zany sense of humor.
Each sketch is zanier than the last.

entries.meaning: Working for something with great, sometimes excessive energy. ---
examples: He is zealous about recycling.
Zealous fans camped out overnight for tickets.
The most zealous reformers went too far.
entries.contrast: Note the vowel: /ˈzɛləs/, even though zeal is /ziːl/.

entries.meaning: Sharp and lively in flavor, or full of energy. ---
examples: The dressing is light and zesty.
Add lime to make the salsa zestier.
It is a zesty little tune for the opening credits.

entries.meaning: Made of short sharp turns, first one way and then the other. ---
examples: The sweater has a zigzag pattern across the chest.
A zigzag path leads down to the water.
He drew a zigzag line under the title.
entries.position: attributive only — before a noun: a zigzag pattern
entries.contrast: Also a verb (the trail zigzags up the hill) and a noun. As an adjective it only goes before a noun.

entries.meaning: From Zimbabwe, or having to do with Zimbabwe. ---
examples: The Zimbabwean dollar collapsed in 2008.
He is a Zimbabwean novelist living in Texas.
Two of the players are Zimbabwean.
entries.contrast: Also a noun for the person: a Zimbabwean. Always capitalized.

entries.meaning: Supporting a Jewish national state in Israel, or having to do with that movement. ---
examples: The book covers the early Zionist movement in Europe.
He writes from an openly Zionist point of view.
Zionist and anti-Zionist groups held rival rallies.
entries.contrast: Capitalized. It names support for a Jewish state in Israel, and it is a political label that some speakers use as an insult, so the speaker matters.

entries.meaning: Fast and lively. ---
examples: It is a zippy little car for city driving.
The new laptop is zippier than my old one.
She gave a zippy two-minute summary.

entries.meaning: Having to do with the scientific study of animals. ---
examples: The zoological garden opened in 1891.
She published a zoological survey of the island.
It is a zoological term, not an everyday one.
entries.position: attributive only — before a noun: a zoological survey
entries.contrast: Watch the first syllables: /ˌzoʊə-/, two syllables, not the /zuː/ of zoo.

entries.meaning: Of a disease that spreads from animals to people.
examples: Rabies is a zoonotic disease.
Most new epidemics are zoonotic in origin.
They study zoonotic spillover in bat populations.
entries.form: from zoonosis, a disease that passes from animals to people
